quizzes.title: Quick quiz
quizzes.question: What is an agent composed of? Pick one.

options.text: Multiple LLM models working in parallel with distributed computing resources
A database system with query optimization capabilities
An LLM combined with a harness
A neural network trained on specific task data

quizzes.explanation: Click an answer. The other three are real things — none of them is an agent.
quizzes.speaker_note: Show of hands before anyone clicks, and let the room commit. Three is right: an agent is an LLM plus a harness. The three wrong answers are each a real thing that people confuse with an agent, so name them as you dismiss them — one is a serving-and-scale answer, two is a database, four is a fine-tuned model. None of them buys you memory, recovery, tools or a human gate, which is exactly the point of the whole talk. On screen the answers colour in on click; in the PDF and .pptx the right one is marked, so the handout still teaches.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz, again
quizzes.question: Two products, same model underneath. One is better. Why? Pick one.

options.text: The speed of model inference
The choice of the latest foundational model
The quality of the harness implementation
The volume of training data used

quizzes.explanation: Everyone can rent the same model. Almost nobody has the same harness. That is where the difference lives — and it is the whole reason this talk exists.
quizzes.speaker_note: The thesis of the talk, as a question. Three is right. Say the uncomfortable part plainly: the model is largely a commodity — your competitor can rent the same one this afternoon, and a better one lands every few months regardless of what either of you does. What you actually control is everything around it. Two is the tempting wrong answer and worth dwelling on, because chasing the newest model is how teams spend a year without shipping anything that survives contact with a user. One and four are the answers of someone still thinking about training rather than about running a product.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — what the loop is for
quizzes.question: What is an agent loop actually doing? Pick one.

options.text: Storing tool results in a database
Running one tool call and returning the result straight away
Validating the format of user input
Going round again — calling tools until the model has enough to answer confidently

quizzes.explanation: Two is the one to argue about: that is a function call, not an agent. The loop is the difference — the model gets to look at what came back and decide it needs something else.
quizzes.speaker_note: Four is right, and two is the answer worth spending time on because it is nearly right. Calling a tool once and returning the answer is a function call with extra ceremony; what makes it an agent is that the result comes BACK into the model, which then decides whether it has enough or needs to go again. That is the whole loop from the earlier slide. Tie it back: this is also why nothing makes it stop on its own, and why a bound belongs in the harness rather than in the prompt.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — why that loop is not enough
quizzes.question: It runs. Why can you not ship it? Pick one.

options.text: It can only work with one tool at a time
It processes data too slowly
It needs too much memory
No error handling, nobody approves the risky bits, and nothing controls it

quizzes.explanation: Notice what is not on the list: speed, memory, and how many tools it can hold. Nothing wrong with that loop is a performance problem.
quizzes.speaker_note: Four is right, and the shape of the wrong answers is the lesson. One, two and three are all performance complaints, and performance is not what stops that loop reaching production — it will happily run fast, all the way into refunding a customer nobody approved. This is the point to make once and hard: the gap between a demo agent and a shipped one is almost never the model or the speed, it is everything the loop does not do when something goes wrong. Refer back to the earlier slide and count them off again if the room needs it.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — the step limit
quizzes.question: Why does an agent workflow need a maximum number of steps? Pick one.

options.text: To cap the characters in each message
To stop the loop running away and burning time and money
To cap how many tools can be registered
To count tokens

quizzes.explanation: Remember the very first loop we looked at: while True, with nothing to stop it. This is that bound.
quizzes.speaker_note: Two is right, and it closes the loop opened by the naive-loop slide — that while True with no exit was the first thing wrong with it, and a step cap is the smallest possible fix. Make the point that the bound belongs in the harness and not in the prompt: asking a model nicely to stop after five turns is a request, whereas a counter in your loop is a guarantee. It is also the cheapest of all seven patterns to add and the one most often missing, because nothing goes wrong until the day something does and the bill arrives.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — no tool calls
quizzes.question: The model comes back with zero tool calls. What does that mean? Pick one.

options.text: The step limit has been reached
Something errored and needs logging
It needs to retry
It has nothing left to do — this is the answer, and the loop is finished

quizzes.explanation: This is the one clean way out of the loop. Everything else that stops it is a failure wearing a result.
quizzes.speaker_note: Four is right. No tool calls means the model has stopped working and started answering, which is the loop's natural exit. Contrast it immediately with option one, because that is the other exit and it is not success — the step cap stopping you is a run that was cut off. Both leave the loop holding some text; only this one means the task is done.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — the failure event
quizzes.question: Why emit a "workflow failed" event when the loop exits? Pick one.

options.text: For debug logging
To record that it hit the step cap or errored — it did not finish
To fail over to a different model provider
To restart the agent

quizzes.explanation: Someone has to be told the difference between done and stopped. If nothing emits that, a cut-off run looks exactly like a finished one.
quizzes.speaker_note: Two is right. This is the previous two slides made operational: your code knows which exit it took, and the event is how everything downstream finds out. Without it a truncated run and a completed run are indistinguishable to a dashboard, a retry policy, or the person waiting on the answer. Tie it to the emit slide — announce what happened, do not wait for anyone — and to the honest point that this repo has no event layer, so it has no way to tell anyone either.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — the loop
quizzes.question: What is the runtime file for? Pick one.

options.text: To store API keys and configuration
To manage database connections and long-term storage
To define the available AI models
The core environment where the agent runs — a game loop, for an agent

quizzes.explanation: Careful with the word: in this deck "the runtime" has meant the whole harness. In many codebases it is also the name of the one file holding the loop.
quizzes.speaker_note: Four is right. Every wrong option is a real file that exists in most projects — config, a database layer, a model registry — which is what makes the question worth asking: the runtime is none of them, it is the loop itself. Flag the naming clash out loud, because this deck has used 'the runtime' since slide 4 to mean the entire harness, and a student who has just read someone else's codebase will have met it as a filename. Both usages are common; what matters is that they notice the ambiguity rather than silently pick one.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — the unfinished conversation
quizzes.question: You resend a message list that ends mid-exchange — a tool call with no result yet. What does the model do? Pick one.

options.text: Errors, because the list is malformed
Returns the last message unchanged
Sees the exchange is unfinished and carries on from there
Starts the conversation again from the top

quizzes.explanation: Which is why resuming is simpler than it sounds: hand back the list and the model works out where it was. The conversation is the state.
quizzes.speaker_note: Three is right, and it is the quietly elegant part of all this. A message list that ends on an assistant turn asking for a tool, with no tool result after it, is visibly incomplete — and the model responds to that by continuing rather than complaining. So recovery does not need a special resume protocol: you load the messages you saved, hand them back, and the model picks up the thread. Tie it to the earlier card — the list is the memory — and to durable execution: what you are persisting IS the conversation, which is why restoring it is enough to carry on. Worth adding the caution: that only works if what you saved is complete and well-formed, which is exactly why you append the finished message rather than a half-streamed one.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — tool calling
quizzes.question: What is tool calling? Pick one.

options.text: A built-in way for a model to reach external functions and APIs
A logging system
A debugging feature
A performance optimisation for multi-region systems

quizzes.explanation: This is how a model stops being a text box. It is also why pattern 3 exists — the moment it can call things, something has to decide what it is allowed to call, and run it somewhere safe.
quizzes.speaker_note: One is right. Worth linking forward rather than treating as a definition: tool calling is the capability that makes every other pattern in this talk necessary. A model that only emits text needs no sandbox, no approval gate and no audit trail. The moment it can call a function, it can spend money, delete a row, or send an email — which is why isolation is pattern 3 and asking a person is pattern 7. The model proposes the call; the harness decides whether it happens.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — the tool description
quizzes.question: What is the description field in a tool definition for? Pick one.

options.text: Validating input parameters
Generating API documentation
Helping the model decide when to call the tool
Documentation for the developers who maintain the code later

quizzes.explanation: Four is the tempting one, and it is why so many tool descriptions are useless. The description is written for the model, not for you.
quizzes.speaker_note: Three is right, and four is the answer most engineers give on instinct because that is what a description field means everywhere else in their working life. Say it plainly: this string is part of the prompt. The model reads it at decision time to work out whether this tool is the one it wants. Write it for the model — plain language, when to use it and when not to — and treat a wrong tool call as a documentation bug, because usually it is. If someone pushes back that a decent model infers most fields anyway, agree: it does, for the obvious ones. The descriptions that earn their keep are on the fields where the NAME does not carry the meaning — an ambiguous label, a term your company uses differently from everyone else, or a value the agent has to look up somewhere else before it can fill this one in. And say the honest part: how much you can rely on inference varies by model, so the weaker the model, the more the description is doing.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — the input schema
quizzes.question: And what is the input schema for? Pick one.

options.text: Encrypting sensitive data
A contract for the arguments the agent has to supply when it calls the tool
Compressing data
Generating user interface components

quizzes.explanation: Description says when to call it. Schema says what has to be in the call. Between them, most bad tool calls stop being possible.
quizzes.speaker_note: Two is right. Pair it with the previous slide and the two together become one idea: the description decides whether the tool gets called at all, and the schema decides whether the call is well-formed. A model that hallucinates an argument name gets rejected by the schema rather than reaching your function — which is the same instinct as pattern 1, a check before the thing runs, moved one layer in. Worth noting for the professionals: this is also the boundary you version, because loosening a schema is how a tool quietly grows capabilities nobody reviewed.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — describing the fields
quizzes.question: Why bother describing each field in the schema? Pick one.

options.text: Documentation for humans only — models cannot read them
So CSS frameworks can style the form
To tell the agent what the field means, when the name alone does not
To make the file bigger

quizzes.explanation: A model will guess item_id. It will not guess a name your company uses oddly, or a value it has to fetch from somewhere else first. Describe those.
quizzes.speaker_note: Three is right and the wrong answers are deliberately silly, so use the time on the nuance instead of the elimination. The honest version: a decent model infers the obvious fields perfectly well, so descriptions are not uniform effort. They earn their keep exactly where the name does not carry the meaning — an ambiguous label, a term that means one thing in your system and another everywhere else, or a field whose value has to be looked up before it can be filled in. And how far you can lean on inference varies by model, so the weaker the model, the harder the description is working.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — what is in a tool call
quizzes.question: The model asks for a tool. What comes back? Pick one.

options.text: A call id, the tool name, and the arguments
Just a call id
Id, name, arguments and an execution timestamp
Just the name and the arguments

quizzes.explanation: Three is the tempting one: there is no timestamp, because nothing has executed yet. This is a request, not a record. The timestamp is yours to add, when you run it.
quizzes.speaker_note: One is right, and three is worth the time because getting it wrong reveals the wrong mental model. A tool call is a REQUEST — a name, some arguments, and an id to match the answer to. There is no execution timestamp in it because nothing has run; the model has asked, and that is all. If you want to know when it actually happened, you record that on your side when you run it, which is the same boundary as everything else in this talk. Tie it back to the round trip: name and arguments say what to do, the id says which question this answers.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — where the tool runs
quizzes.question: The model asks for a tool call. Where does it actually run? Pick one.

options.text: In the browser
In cloud storage
On the model provider's servers, automatically
On your own server, after the model asks for it

quizzes.explanation: Three is the belief worth correcting today. The provider has no copy of your code. And that is good news — it is why a guardrail or a human gate can exist at all.
quizzes.speaker_note: Four is right, and three is a genuinely common misconception that is worth killing in the room. The provider does not have your function, cannot run it, and never sees it — all it gets is a name, a schema and a description. Everything actually happens on your side. Frame that as the good news rather than a limitation: because execution is yours, you get to decide whether a call happens at all, put it in a sandbox, bound it with a clock, or stop and ask a person. If the provider ran your tools, none of the seven patterns would be available to you.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — the call id
quizzes.question: Why does a tool call carry an id? Pick one.

options.text: To authenticate the tool with the provider
To encrypt the message
So the result can be matched back to the request that asked for it
To store tool calls for auditing

quizzes.explanation: Send several calls at once and the answers come back out of order. The id is how anything makes sense of that. Drop it and most models break outright.
quizzes.speaker_note: Three is right. It sounds like plumbing until you picture more than one call in flight: the model asked three things, three results come back, and without an id nothing tells it which answer belongs to which question. That is why it is not optional — most providers will error rather than guess. Worth linking to pattern 6: the moment you fan work out, correlating replies to requests stops being a detail and becomes the whole job, and this is the smallest version of that problem.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — sending a result back
quizzes.question: You ran the tool. Which role carries the result back to the model? Pick one.

options.text: user — it is going into the conversation
assistant — it belongs with the call that asked
tool — with the id of the call it answers
system — it is machine output

quizzes.explanation: The roles are not decoration. Put a tool result in as the user and you have just told the model a person said it — which is exactly the confusion pattern 1 exists to prevent.
quizzes.speaker_note: Three is right, and the reason is worth more than the fact. Roles are a trust boundary, not labels: system is you, user is the person, assistant is the model, tool is machine output from something the model asked for. Smuggle a tool result in under the user role — which people do, because it is easy — and you have told the model a human said it, which is the same category of confusion that prompt injection exploits. The id goes with it so the model knows which of its questions this answers.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — what has to be last
quizzes.question: You have built the list and you are about to call the model. What must be on the end of it? Pick one.

options.text: Something waiting on an answer — the person’s message, or a tool result
The standing instructions, repeated at the bottom
An empty message, to show the turn is over
A sample reply, to show it the format you want

quizzes.explanation: The list is a question, and the last line is the question. End on the model’s own previous reply and you have handed it nothing to respond to. Standing instructions go at the top and stay there — putting them last does not make them louder.
quizzes.speaker_note: One. This is a small thing that produces very confusing bugs, so it earns a slide. The message list is not a transcript you are archiving, it is a question you are asking, and the last entry is the actual question. So it has to be something that leaves the model with work to do: the person's new message, or the result of a tool it just asked for. End on the assistant's own last reply and you have asked it to respond to itself — some providers error, others produce something odd and directionless, and either way the fault is several layers from where it looks. Kill option two while you are here, because it is the tempting one: standing instructions belong at the top, in the system role, and repeating them at the bottom to make them stick is a habit worth unlearning — it costs tokens every turn and does not buy obedience. Option four is a real technique in the wrong place; showing the model examples of the format you want is fine, but they belong in the instructions as examples, not dangling at the end where a genuine question should be. Tie it back to the round trip: when a tool result goes on the end, that is the loop closing, and the model now has exactly what it asked for and a reason to speak again.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — the roles
quizzes.question: What are the four roles in a message list? Pick one.

options.text: prompt, response, context, function
admin, client, server, callback
input, output, error, response
system, user, assistant, tool

quizzes.explanation: The whole conversation is just that list, replayed every turn. Which is why it costs what it costs.
quizzes.speaker_note: Four is right. Walk them: system is your standing instructions, user is what the person typed, assistant is what the model said, tool carries results back from a call you ran. Two things fall out. The conversation is not held anywhere clever — it is a list you resend in full on every single turn, which is exactly why memory and summarising matter and why the system prompt is not free. And the roles are a trust boundary, not just a label: prompt injection is user text trying to be read as system text, which is why pattern 1 checks the input rather than trusting the roles to hold on their own.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — the message list
quizzes.question: Why append every reply back onto the list? Pick one.

options.text: The model keeps no memory of previous turns — you resend everything, every time
To make later queries faster
To reduce API costs
To make streaming work

quizzes.explanation: Two and three are not just wrong, they are backwards: a longer list is slower and dearer. You pay for the memory, every single turn.
quizzes.speaker_note: One is right. The provider holds nothing between calls — the whole conversation goes up with every request, which is why the list IS the memory and why forgetting to append leaves the model with no idea it ever spoke. Land the sting in the small print: the two plausible-sounding wrong answers claim a benefit, and the truth is the exact opposite. Every turn you keep costs you again. That is the thread back to pattern 4 — summarising is not tidying, it is cost control.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — as the list grows
quizzes.question: The conversation gets longer. What happens? Pick one.

options.text: Nothing changes
It costs more, but runs just as fast
It costs more and gets slower
It improves — the model learns from the history

quizzes.explanation: Four is the comfortable myth. Nothing is being learned; the same text is simply being read again, from scratch, on every turn. That is what you are paying for.
quizzes.speaker_note: Three is right, and four is worth a moment because it is a genuinely widespread misunderstanding: nothing is learned from a conversation. The model is not improving as you talk to it — it is re-reading the same growing pile of text on each call, which costs more tokens and takes longer. Both curves go the wrong way together. This is the whole economic argument for pattern 4: recent turns verbatim, older ones summarised, and the bulk of what you know kept outside the conversation in a store you query.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — streaming
quizzes.question: What does a streaming text call do? Pick one.

options.text: Sends the messages and streams the reply back token by token
Stores the conversation in a database
Compresses data
Validates the input before it reaches the model

quizzes.explanation: It is not faster. The words arrive at the same rate either way — but a blank screen for twenty seconds reads as a crash, and streaming lets someone stop a bad answer early.
quizzes.speaker_note: One is right. The point to make is that this is a user-experience decision, not a performance one: the total time to a finished answer is unchanged, but the perceived wait collapses, and a reader can abandon an answer that is clearly going wrong instead of paying for all of it. If you want the whole thing at once instead, that is the generate call rather than the stream call — same request, different shape of return. This repo does not stream; its API answers in one go.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — waiting for the stream
quizzes.question: Why wait for the stream to finish before appending? Pick one.

options.text: Browser compatibility
To prevent memory leaks
To optimise the connection
So you append the finished message, not half of one

quizzes.explanation: A half-streamed reply pushed into the history is not a rendering glitch. The next turn reads it as something the agent actually said.
quizzes.speaker_note: Four is right. Streaming is for the human watching; the history is for the model, and the model needs the completed message. Push it early and you have written a truncated sentence into the permanent record of the conversation, which the next turn then treats as settled. Worth saying that this is a nice illustration of the difference between the two audiences a harness serves at once — the person, who wants to see progress, and the model, which wants a clean transcript.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — swapping model providers
quizzes.question: How does the Vercel AI SDK support multiple providers? Pick one.

options.text: A separate module per provider, all working with the same methods like streamText or generateText
Runtime configuration files edited by hand for each switch
Separate API calls per provider
A universal API key

quizzes.explanation: Different ecosystem, the same trick worth stealing: one agreed shape, many implementations behind it. Change the import, not the code that calls it. We do it with a Protocol; they do it with a module per provider.
quizzes.speaker_note: One is right, and this is a gift of a slide for a professional audience because it is the seam pattern in someone else's language. The AI SDK ships @ai-sdk/openai, @ai-sdk/anthropic and so on; each exports something that satisfies the same interface, so streamText and generateText do not change when you switch. That is exactly our CheckpointStore Protocol, and exactly why the deck argues the trick is worth stealing rather than being a Python detail. Be clear this project does NOT use the AI SDK — it is Python on the Microsoft Agent Framework. The point is the shape of the idea, not the tool.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — the system prompt
quizzes.question: What is a system prompt? Pick one.

options.text: A debugging tool that traces the agent's decisions
The error shown when the agent fails
The user's question that starts the conversation
The standing instructions that define how the agent behaves

quizzes.explanation: Three is the near-miss worth naming: that is the user message. The system prompt comes from whoever built the agent, and the user never sees it.
quizzes.speaker_note: Four is right, and three is the one to talk about — the difference between what the builder says and what the user says is the whole trust model. The system prompt is yours, arrives before anything the user types, and defines persona, context and rules. Two things follow. It is not free: thousands of tokens on every turn, which is the same budget argument as the knowledge base. And it is not a security boundary: a prompt-injection attack is precisely an attempt to get user text treated as though it were system text, which is why pattern 1 checks the input rather than trusting the instructions to hold.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — idempotency
quizzes.question: Why must a step be safe to run more than once? Pick one.

options.text: It compresses data
It reduces latency
So running it twice gives the same result, with no second side effect
It scales the system horizontally

quizzes.explanation: "Work out the total" twice is harmless. "Send the money" twice is not. The save comes after the step, so that gap is real.
quizzes.speaker_note: Three is right, and it is the one piece of durable execution that people skip until it bites. The checkpoint goes down after the step runs, so a crash in that window means the step runs again on resume — at-least-once, which is what nearly every durable system actually offers. Harmless for a calculation, expensive for a payment or an email. The fix is in the action, not the checkpoint: make it repeat-safe, usually by handing the downstream system a key it can deduplicate on. Say plainly that our own run_durably has exactly this window.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — you already use one
quizzes.question: What makes CI/CD a distributed system you already know? Pick one.

options.text: It runs elsewhere, talks back to other systems, and updates status whether or not you are watching
It uses AI to write the tests
It needs someone to press the buttons
It only runs locally

quizzes.explanation: Stages you can retry. Caching between them. Status that arrives whether the tab is open or not. Recovery when a runner dies. You have been using durable execution for years.
quizzes.speaker_note: One is right, and this is the most useful analogy in the whole durable-execution section because everyone in the room has already lived it. A pipeline runs somewhere else, reports back to GitHub, has stages you can replay individually, caches between them, and updates status asynchronously whether or not anyone is looking. When a runner dies you do not start the release from scratch. Every property we want from a durable agent workflow is something they already expect from CI — so the pattern is not exotic, it is just unfamiliar in this context.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — where the save points live
quizzes.question: Durable-execution tools exist to do what? Pick one.

options.text: Handle authentication
Replace the database with an in-memory cache
Compile code faster
Keep every step's inputs and outputs in a database, so a run can resume

quizzes.explanation: Wrap an operation in a step and its inputs and outputs are recorded — so a replay skips it rather than redoing it. Several tools do this — Temporal, Inngest, DBOS — and the Agent Framework has its own, which is what this repo runs. Ours is a seam: a file on a laptop today, a cloud database later.
quizzes.speaker_note: Four is right, and the mechanism is worth a sentence: wrapping an operation in a step records its inputs AND its outputs, which is what lets a replay skip a finished step instead of running it again. That is a stronger guarantee than our own run_durably, which only saves state after each step. But do not oversell it — people say this 'prevents duplicate execution', and it does only once the record has landed. Crash between doing the thing and recording that you did it and you are back to at-least-once, which is why idempotent steps matter even with a good engine underneath. The category is durable execution and there are a handful of real options — DBOS, Temporal, Inngest, Upstash, Cloudflare Workflows — which differ mostly in how much infrastructure they demand. The database-backed ones are the easy sell because you probably already have a database, and the change to your code is small. Tie it back to the seam: we did not pick one. CheckpointStore is a shape with a SQLite implementation behind it, so choosing a real engine later is an implementation swap rather than a rewrite. That is the whole argument for writing the interface down first.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — the client goes away
quizzes.question: Someone closes the tab mid-conversation, then comes back. What should happen? Pick one.

options.text: Throw the context away, for security
Pick up where they left off
Start again from the beginning
Wait for someone to intervene

quizzes.explanation: The work does not belong to the connection. On reconnect you replay the log to them — which is what the sequence numbers were for — and they catch up to wherever the run got to. This is the crash demo again, except nothing crashed; someone just left.
quizzes.speaker_note: Two is right, and it is worth pointing out that this is the same machinery as the crash demo wearing different clothes. Nothing failed here; a person shut a laptop. If the run lives in the connection, closing the tab kills it and they come back to nothing — which is precisely the experience that makes people distrust these products. If the run lives in a save point, the connection is just a window onto work that carried on regardless. That is also why the transport has to push rather than only answer: when they return, the result may have been ready for ten minutes.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — what deserves a save point?
quizzes.question: You cannot save after every line. Which of these is worth wrapping? Pick one.

options.text: Adding up numbers you already have in front of you
Anything that reaches out of your process — slow, unrepeatable, or paid for
Every line, to be safe
Only writes to the database

quizzes.explanation: Three questions, and any yes means wrap it: does it leave your process and take time? Would it answer differently if you ran it again? Did it cost money? Pure local arithmetic needs none of it — a replay will work it out again, identically, for nothing.
quizzes.speaker_note: Two. This is the question everybody actually has when they meet durable execution — not what a step is, but which things should be one — so give them the test as three questions they can run in their head. Does it leave the process? Anything crossing the boundary is slow and can fail independently of you: an API call, a database write, a file, a payment. Would it answer differently next time? That is the model call, anything with a clock or a random number in it, anything reading state someone else can change. Did it cost money? Then re-buying it on every resume is waste you chose. Any single yes is enough. And say what does NOT need wrapping, because over-wrapping is the other failure and it makes a workflow unreadable: pure computation over data you already hold is free to redo and will produce exactly the same answer, so recording it buys you nothing but noise. The neat part is that the three criteria are the same three arguments the deck has already made separately — the model call is the non-deterministic one, the emit paired with its operation is the leaves-your-process one, and the expensive-call argument is the third. This slide is just the rule they all came from.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — making a step durable
quizzes.question: How do you turn an ordinary operation into a recorded step? Pick one.

options.text: Add it to a workflow configuration object first
Register it up front, before the workflow runs
Create it with a name and a handler
Wrap the operation, passing the work in as a function

quizzes.explanation: Learn the shape, not the spelling. Wrapping means the library sees the call happen, so it can record what went in and what came out. Registering it somewhere else could not.
quizzes.speaker_note: Four is right, and the small print is the transferable part — the exact method name differs by library and does not matter. What matters is why it is a wrapper rather than a registration: the library has to be inside the call to see its inputs and its result, and to know whether it finished. A step declared in a config file somewhere is just a name; a step that wraps the work can record it. That is the same reason the deck keeps returning to who is executing — recording, bounding and approving all require being in the path, not adjacent to it. This project does not use DBOS; its CheckpointStore seam is the same idea one layer down.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — the model call in a step
quizzes.question: Why wrap the call to the model itself in a step? Pick one.

options.text: So a restart does not buy the same expensive call twice
To turn a synchronous call asynchronous
To make the model faster by caching in memory
To run several model calls in parallel

quizzes.explanation: Right — and there is a second reason that matters more. The model is not deterministic: ask again and it may answer differently and send the run down another path. Recording the answer is what makes a replay a replay.
quizzes.speaker_note: One is right and it is the answer everyone gives, so use the small print to go past it. Cost is real but shallow. The deeper reason is determinism: a recorded step replays the answer the run actually got, whereas re-calling the model during recovery can produce a different answer, a different tool choice, a different branch — at which point you are not resuming a run, you are starting a divergent one with the same id. That is much harder to notice than a bill. Say both, in that order, and the room will remember the second one.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — emits in a step
quizzes.question: Why put the emit inside a step rather than loose in the workflow? Pick one.

options.text: To broadcast events in real time
So a restart cannot fire it a second time
To improve performance
To get database transaction guarantees

quizzes.explanation: An emit left loose in the workflow is not recorded, so a resume runs it again — and now the log says a thing happened twice that only happened once. Anything with an effect belongs in a step.
quizzes.speaker_note: Two is right. The general rule is the one to leave them with: in a durable workflow, anything with an effect on the outside world belongs inside a step, because a step is the only thing that gets recorded and therefore the only thing a resume will skip. Code sitting loose between steps runs again on every recovery. For an emit that means duplicate events in your own audit trail, which is worse than it sounds — the record is supposed to be the thing you trust when you are reconstructing what happened. Same rule covers sending mail, taking payment, or writing a row.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — awaiting a streaming step
quizzes.question: You wrap a streaming call in a step and await it. Does the streaming stop? Pick one.

options.text: Yes — awaiting collects it all before anything is shown
No — the stream still runs inside; you are waiting for the step to finish
Only if the database is slow
Streaming cannot be used in a durable workflow

quizzes.explanation: You are awaiting the step, not the first token. Tokens flow to the reader exactly as before; the step simply records what happened once it is done.
quizzes.speaker_note: Two is right, and it removes a fear that stops people adopting durable execution at all — the belief that making something durable must make it feel slower. It does not. Awaiting the step means waiting for that unit of work to complete, while the streaming inside it goes on doing what it always did, token by token, to whoever is watching. The two concerns are simply at different layers: streaming is how the human experiences the call, the step is how the system records it.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — when do you need a sandbox?
quizzes.question: Two situations make it unavoidable. Which pair? Pick one.

options.text: Long conversations, and large files
When it runs risky code — shell, SQL — and when it writes programs that chain tools together
When there are many users, and when latency matters
Only when handling payments

quizzes.explanation: A coding agent running shell. An analysis agent running SQL. And code mode, where it writes a program instead of picking from a menu. A menu is a bounded set of asks. A program is not.
quizzes.speaker_note: Two is right. Both cases share a shape: the agent stops choosing from things you predefined and starts producing something arbitrary. A coding agent that runs shell commands, or an analysis agent writing SQL, is executing text the model composed — and code mode is the same thing generalised, where it writes a short program stringing several tools together instead of spending a turn on each. That second one is genuinely better engineering, faster and cheaper, and it is exactly what removes your ability to enumerate what might happen. Hence the stranger line from the pattern slide: you would not give an unknown person shell on production, and an arbitrary program from a model is the same risk with better manners.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — why code mode wins
quizzes.question: What does writing code buy over calling tools one at a time? Pick one.

options.text: It combines several tools into one execution, so a dozen turns become one
It removes the need for a model at all
It generates documentation and an audit trail
It needs fewer logins

quizzes.explanation: Sequential calling is ask, wait, think, ask again — every hop costing a round trip and a pile of tokens. A program does the whole errand and comes back once.
quizzes.speaker_note: One is right. Picture the sequential version honestly: call a tool, wait, reason about what came back, call the next, wait again — a task needing a dozen lookups is a dozen round trips, each one paying for the whole conversation again in tokens. Code mode collapses that into a single execution that loops and combines on its own and returns the finished answer. The catch, which is the reason pattern 3 exists, is that you have traded a bounded menu of tool calls for an arbitrary program.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — who needs to run code?
quizzes.question: Which agents actually benefit from being able to execute code? Pick one.

options.text: Ones handling logins, to run security checks
Ones doing analysis or writing software — real computation
Ones that only summarise text
Ones generating images

quizzes.explanation: If the job is working something out, code earns its place. If the job is producing prose, it is a liability you did not need. Do not hand out a capability the task never asked for.
quizzes.speaker_note: Two is right, and the closing line is the transferable rule. Analysis and coding agents genuinely need to compute — filter a dataset, solve an equation, run a query — and code is how they do it accurately. A summarising agent does not, and giving it the capability anyway buys you every risk of pattern 3 in exchange for nothing. That is worth saying plainly to a room full of people about to build their first agent: the temptation is to hand it everything you can, and each capability you add is a boundary you now have to defend. Start with what the task requires.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — arithmetic
quizzes.question: Why let the agent write code for a calculation instead of working it out? Pick one.

options.text: So it can avoid using any maths libraries
So it learns maths by trial and error
Code is deterministic — it gets the same right answer every time
It halves the memory footprint

quizzes.explanation: A model doing arithmetic is predicting what the answer looks like. Code is computing it. Dates are the worst case — “how many working days between these two” reads as a language question and is not one. For anything that has one correct answer, do not ask a guesser.
quizzes.speaker_note: Three is right, and it generalises far past arithmetic. The model is a prediction machine; asked for the roots of a quadratic it produces text that looks like the roots of a quadratic, which is usually right and occasionally, silently, is not. Handing the same job to code changes the kind of thing it is — a computation with one answer, repeatable, checkable. The rule worth leaving them with: anything with exactly one correct answer should be computed rather than predicted, and the agent's job is deciding to run it, not being the calculator. Dates are the sharpest example to say out loud, because everyone has been bitten: ask how many working days sit between two dates and you get a fluent, confident, plausible number that is wrong often enough to matter, because the question looks like language and is actually calendar arithmetic with leap years and bank holidays in it. Note what the split really is — the model is genuinely good at WRITING the code that does this and genuinely bad at BEING it, so play to that: let it generate, let the runtime compute. This is the same instinct behind the sealed-numbers rule in a lot of regulated work — the model writes the words, the arithmetic comes from somewhere that can be audited.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — why dates in particular
quizzes.question: A model is worse at dates than at almost any other everyday thing. Why? Pick one.

options.text: Date formats vary from country to country
It never sees the date as a date — it gets chopped into fragments that mean nothing on their own
It has never been shown a calendar
Too many digits, and digits cause mistakes

quizzes.explanation: A model reads text in chunks, and 2026-08-25 may arrive as pieces like 202, 6, -08. Nothing in there says “August”, or “a Tuesday”, or “31 days”. It is reassembling a calendar from crumbs, every time.
quizzes.speaker_note: Two. And this is the one slide that explains a weakness people otherwise find baffling — something that can discuss constitutional law cannot reliably tell you what day of the week a date falls on. The reason is underneath the language: text is split into chunks before the model ever sees it, and a date does not survive that split intact. It arrives as fragments that carry no calendar meaning at all. Nothing in the pieces encodes that this is August, that August has 31 days, that the year is a leap year, or where the weekend falls. Be honest that tokenisation is not the whole story, because a sharp student will push on it: even given a perfectly clean date, the model has no calendar algorithm to execute and no dependable way to carry a multi-step calculation across several steps. So the tokenisation is why it starts badly and the lack of a procedure is why it does not recover. Both point the same way — do not ask it to compute the date, ask it to write the two lines of code that compute the date. That is the whole of pattern 3 in one example, and it is the example to use if you only have time for one.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — a bigger window
quizzes.question: Your conversation keeps growing. You move to a model with a huge context window. Problem solved? Pick one.

options.text: Yes — room for everything, so nothing needs managing
No — it gets slower, costs more, and quietly loses the middle
Yes, as long as you stay under the limit
No, because long conversations are refused outright

quizzes.explanation: You resend the whole conversation every turn, so it gets slower and dearer with every message. Worse, attention is not even: the start and the end land, the middle fades. A bigger window buys you room, not reliability — which is why you summarise, and keep the bulk in a store you query.
quizzes.speaker_note: Two, and this is the slide that stops someone solving pattern 4 by buying a bigger number. Three things go wrong together as a conversation grows and only one of them is obvious. It gets slower, because the whole history is resent every single turn — there is no server-side memory of your chat unless something is deliberately keeping it. It gets more expensive for the same reason, and over a long session the cost compounds rather than staying flat, because every turn pays for every turn before it. And the one nobody predicts: it gets less accurate. Attention across a long context is not uniform — material at the beginning and the end is used well, material in the middle is measurably less likely to be used at all, which is why people talk about losing the middle. Be fair about the caveat if a sharp student pushes: this was first measured on earlier long-context models and newer ones handle it better, so it is a real effect that varies by model, not a fixed law. The conclusion survives either way. A bigger window is more room, not more reliability, and it does nothing about the cost curve. So you summarise what is old and keep the bulk outside in something you query. That is pattern 4, and this is the argument for it.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — what you are allowed to drop
quizzes.question: The history is too long, so something has to go. What is the smallest piece you can safely remove? Pick one.

options.text: Any single message — oldest first
A whole turn — the request and every tool result it was waiting on
Any two messages, to keep the count even
Half the list, whenever it gets too long

quizzes.explanation: A tool call and its result are joined by an id, and the result must come immediately after — nothing may be slipped in between. Cut between them and you leave a question with no answer — most models reject the list outright, and the ones that do not get confused. So you group the messages into turns, add up the whole lot to see if you are over, and roll up entire turns.
quizzes.speaker_note: Two. This is the practical detail that turns compaction from an idea into working code, and it is where people's first attempt breaks. The instinct is to treat the history as a list of messages and drop from the front until it fits. That produces a broken list, because messages are not independent: an assistant message that asks for a tool and the tool result that answers it are joined by a call id, and they only make sense as a pair. Drop the first and you have a result answering nothing; drop the second and you have a question that was never answered. Most providers reject a list in that state, which is at least honest — the worse case is the one that accepts it and quietly gets strange. So the unit is the turn: the request and every tool result it was waiting on, complete. In practice you hold the history grouped into turns, flatten the whole thing when you want to measure it, and when you are over the limit you roll up entire turns from the old end. Point at the shape they have already seen — this is the same rule as grouping operations into a durable step. The question is never how small you can slice it, it is what stops making sense apart. Split either one down the middle and you get a state your system has no way to interpret.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — the knowledge base
quizzes.question: What is a knowledge base for? Pick one.

options.text: Logging every API call
Caching responses
A body of information the agent looks things up in, instead of carrying it all in the prompt
Storing credentials and tokens

quizzes.explanation: A wiki it queries, not a wiki it pastes. Paste it and every single turn costs you the whole corpus in tokens — for the three paragraphs it actually needed.
quizzes.speaker_note: Three is right, and it is memory pattern 4 seen from the cost side. The reason a fact store is separate from the conversation is economics as much as design: the context window is finite and you pay for it on every turn, so a corpus that lives outside and gets queried — by RAG, or by plain old search — is the only version that scales past a handful of documents. Two is worth a word: caching is a real thing, it is just a different thing. If anyone asks how the agent knows what to look up, that is the retrieval step, and it is exactly where a bad tool description costs you.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — where a handoff has to happen
quizzes.question: You give the agent a “hand over to billing” tool. It calls it. What actually happens? Pick one.

options.text: Billing takes over the conversation
Nothing is handed over — the answer lands back in the same agent, which is still the one talking
Both agents reply from then on
The conversation ends

quizzes.explanation: Record who it went to, who it came from, and why while you are there — a transfer with no reason attached is the one nobody can explain a week later. A tool result always comes back to the agent that asked — that is the whole shape of the loop. Nothing can take itself out of its own conversation and put something else there. Only the layer running the agents can change which one is running, so the tool call is a request to hand over, and the runtime does it.
quizzes.speaker_note: Two, and it is the most commonly got-wrong thing on this whole subject, because the obvious implementation is quietly a no-op. You give the agent a handoff tool, it calls it, and you believe the transfer happened — but look at the loop we drew at the start: a tool result goes back to the agent that requested it, always. So the billing agent never gets the conversation; the original agent gets a message saying billing was notified, and carries on talking. Nothing moved. The reason is worth stating as a principle, because it recurs: nothing can remove itself from its own context and install a replacement. An agent is inside the loop, and the choice of which agent the loop is running sits outside it. So a real handoff is two pieces — the tool call is the agent REQUESTING a transfer, and the runtime around it is what actually swaps who is running. Say the general form out loud, because they have already met it twice today: you cannot make durable, or safe, or transferable, anything you are not the one executing. It was true when we wrapped an operation in a step, and it is true here.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — how many agents do you need?
quizzes.question: You have a genuinely hard problem. How many agents should work on it? Pick one.

options.text: One per step, so each stays simple
Usually one — a good model with a well-built harness around it
At least three, or there is nothing to route between
One per tool

quizzes.explanation: A crowd of agents is the exciting answer and rarely the right one. When you do split, the reason is usually not cleverness: a destructive tool that only one agent may touch, different permissions, or different teams owning different parts. Organisational reasons, mostly — not capability ones.
quizzes.speaker_note: Two, and this is deliberately the sober slide after two patterns about using more than one agent, because the natural conclusion from those is more agents equals better and that is not true. Most problems that look like they need a team of agents are one capable model with a properly built harness around it — which is the entire argument of this talk, so say it plainly: the work is in the harness, not in the headcount. Swarms of agents genuinely earn their place at the very hard end, the kind of open-ended research problem where you want many attempts explored in parallel, and almost nowhere else. Then the useful half, which is the part people have not thought about: when you should split, the reasons are usually organisational rather than technical. One agent may hold the tool that deletes things and no other. Different agents run with different permissions and different guardrails. Different teams own different agents and ship them on their own schedule. Those are real and they are good reasons. Wanting it to feel sophisticated is not. And remember the cost from the previous slide: every extra agent is a config away, which makes it easy to add and quietly expensive to run and to reason about.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — who decides it needs approving?
quizzes.question: A refund over £1,000 must be signed off. Where does that rule live? Pick one.

options.text: In the instructions — tell the model to ask before big refunds
In your code, as a plain rule that runs every time
Give it an “ask a human” tool and let it choose when
Whichever is easier — they amount to the same thing

quizzes.explanation: One and three both leave the gate to a judgement call, and a model that is right ninety-nine times in a hundred still lets one through. An if statement is right every time. Never make the safety of a system depend on the model remembering to be safe.
quizzes.speaker_note: Two, and this is the sharpest single idea in pattern seven, so do not rush it. The tempting answers are one and three, because both look responsible — you told it to ask, or you gave it a tool for asking. But both hand the decision to the model, and the model is a predictor. Ninety-nine times out of a hundred it asks, and the hundredth it just does the refund, and that is precisely the case you built the gate for. A rule in your own code — if the amount is over a thousand, stop and wait — is right every single time, is testable, and is the same tomorrow as it was today. Say the line plainly because it is the one worth taking away from this whole section: never make the safety of a system depend on the model remembering to be safe. Then connect it to the last two slides, because it is the third appearance of one principle. The handoff has to live in the runtime because an agent cannot replace itself. Approval has to live in the runtime because a gate the model can forget is not a gate. Wrapping an operation in a durable step was the same move again. Every time, the answer is that control belongs to the layer doing the running, not to the thing being run — and that layer is the harness. That is the talk.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — the send button
quizzes.question: You give an agent a "send reply" tool and no gate. What is the risk? Pick one.

options.text: It crashes under too many concurrent sends
It gets slower as the queue grows
It emails real people, in your name, before anyone has read the drafts
It costs more in API calls

quizzes.explanation: And it is not misbehaving when it does. You told it to reply to the email; sending is how replying finishes.
quizzes.speaker_note: Three is right, and this is the single best argument for pattern 7 in the whole deck, so give it room. The other three answers are the ones an engineer reaches for — crashes, latency, cost — and none of them is the thing that gets you fired. What makes this example land is that the agent is not broken and has not been jailbroken: it was told to reply to the email, sending is how replying completes, and it completed. That is precisely why the gate cannot live in the prompt. You cannot instruct your way out of an agent doing exactly what you asked. Ask the room which tool in their own system would be dangerous under that reading; someone always names one they had not thought about.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — the sequence number
quizzes.question: Why does every row in an event log carry a sequence number? Pick one.

options.text: To cache frequently accessed data
To hold the database authentication token
To track the order of events, for replay and for spotting duplicates
To encrypt the event

quizzes.explanation: Events arrive late, and sometimes twice. That is normal, not a bug you can engineer away — so the log carries the order itself.
quizzes.speaker_note: Three is right. Two jobs from one integer: replay in the true order, and recognise an event you have already handled. The framing that matters is the small print — out-of-order and duplicate delivery are properties of distributed systems, not defects, so the design has to absorb them rather than wish them away. Tie it to idempotency: the sequence number is how a listener becomes safely repeatable, the same way a dedup key makes a step safely repeatable.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — save, then shout
quizzes.question: When does emit tell the connected clients? Pick one.

options.text: After the event is safely written to the database
Immediately, as soon as emit is called
Before the write, so listeners still get it if the write fails
Only on restart

quizzes.explanation: Three sounds generous and is the dangerous one. Tell people something happened, then fail to record it, and nobody can ever reconcile the two.
quizzes.speaker_note: One is right, and three is the answer worth arguing with because it sounds like resilience. It is the opposite. If you notify before persisting and the write fails, every connected client now believes something your system has no record of — and there is no way to detect the disagreement later, because your log looks perfectly consistent with itself. A slightly slower event is cheap; an unrecorded one that people acted on is not. Same instinct as the human gate: do the irreversible thing last, once the reversible parts have succeeded.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — unsubscribing
quizzes.question: What does subscribe hand back, and why? Pick one.

options.text: The last event, so you can catch up
A function that removes your listener — call it or they pile up
A connection id for logging
Nothing

quizzes.explanation: Every listener you add and never remove is a leak. In a process that runs for weeks, that is how you end up rebooting it every Tuesday.
quizzes.speaker_note: Two is right. Handing the cleanup back with the subscription is a small design choice with a big payoff: the caller cannot forget where the off switch is, because they were given it. Skip it and listeners accumulate — each holding whatever it closed over — which in a long-lived server is a slow leak that looks like a mystery until someone profiles it. Worth naming the general habit: whatever acquires a resource should hand back the way to release it, in the same breath.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — the payload column
quizzes.question: Why hold the event's data as JSON in the database? Pick one.

options.text: It validates the payload against a schema on the way in
Every event carries a different shape, and the database can store JSON directly
It encrypts the column
It compresses long strings

quizzes.explanation: The columns you query — who, what kind, when, which number — get real columns. The bit that differs per event goes in one JSON field. It does not validate anything.
quizzes.speaker_note: Two is right. The shape of an event log is the point: the fields you filter and sort on — run id, event type, timestamp, sequence number — are proper columns, and the payload, which is different for every event type, is one JSON column. That way you get real queries over the structure without inventing forty nullable columns for forty event types. One is the trap and worth killing: a JSON column enforces that the value is valid JSON and nothing more. If you want the payload to match a schema, that check is yours to write — which is the same lesson as the tool input schema, one layer down.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — the transport
quizzes.question: Why WebSockets rather than server-sent events? Pick one.

options.text: They go both ways, so a distributed layer can push results to any connected client
They are required by the SDK
They are faster than HTTP
They use less bandwidth

quizzes.explanation: Speed and bandwidth are not the reason. Direction is: server-sent events only flow one way, so the client could never fire a task and be told about it later.
quizzes.speaker_note: One is right. Two, three and four are all plausible-sounding performance answers, and none of them is why. The reason is structural: SSE is server-to-client only, so it cannot carry fire-and-forget work in the other direction, and a durable distributed layer needs to push a result back to whichever client is connected — possibly not the one that started the job, possibly from a different machine. If someone argues SSE plus a POST would do it, agree that it would, and point out you have now hand-rolled half a WebSocket.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — emit
quizzes.question: What does the emit pattern accomplish? Pick one.

options.text: It compresses data for transmission
It establishes secure connections between servers across regions
It tells anyone interested that an event has occurred
It validates input parameters

quizzes.explanation: And crucially it does not wait for anyone to answer. That is what stops one slow listener from holding up the work.
quizzes.speaker_note: Three is right. The word to stress in the answer is 'anyone' — the emitter does not know or care who is listening, which is exactly what makes the pattern scale and what makes it testable. Add the half the option does not say: it does not wait. A component that blocks until every listener has responded has reinvented a synchronous call with extra steps.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — is anyone still there?
quizzes.question: Before writing to a socket you check its ready state. What are you checking? Pick one.

options.text: Whether the client is an administrator
Whether the connection is still open
Whether the client is authenticated
Whether encryption is on

quizzes.explanation: Clients leave without saying goodbye — closed laptops, dead wifi, shut tabs. Writing into a socket nobody is holding is how a background job takes the server down with it.
quizzes.speaker_note: Two is right. The habit worth teaching is smaller than the API: never assume the other end is still there. Connections die silently — a laptop closes, wifi drops, a tab shuts — and your process finds out only when it tries to write. Check first, and treat a missing client as completely normal rather than an error, because it is. Tie it back: this is precisely why the work must not live in the connection. If the run is durable, a vanished client is a non-event; you keep going and they see the result when they return. If it is not, the disappearance takes the work with it.

quizzes.title: Quick quiz — now apply it
quizzes.question: You are building an agent that trades money. What matters most? Pick one.

options.text: Chat interface design
Self-healing, guardrails, approval steps, and keeping financial data safe
Real-time market charts
File upload

quizzes.explanation: Every wrong answer is about the screen. The right one is the harness — and it is patterns 1, 6 and 7 with money on the line.
quizzes.speaker_note: The applied question, and the best one to end on. Two is right. What makes it land is the shape of the wrong answers: all three are interface features, and all three are what people reach for first when asked to build something that trades. The chart is not what stops a bad trade — a guardrail on the way in, a supervisor that isolates a failing leg, and a human who signs off above a threshold are. Point at the flight-deck slide if you used it: two people and two keys for anything irreversible. And say the honest bit — a real trading harness also needs an audit log you cannot edit, which this repo has as an append-only store but the talk does not cover.
